Stand up vLLM.desc: Everything else in this task is a variation on one server. Get `vllm serve` running with a small open model, hit it through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and learn the four knobs that actually change behaviour — plus how to read the startup log where the engine tells you how much KV cache it managed to allocate.
steps: Install vLLM and run `vllm serve <small-model>` with an explicit `--max-model-len`, then hit `/v1/models` and `/v1/chat/completions` with plain curl before touching any client library.
Read the startup log and find the line reporting the number of KV cache blocks and the resulting maximum concurrency. Write that number down; it is the capacity of your endpoint.
Sweep `--gpu-memory-utilization` from 0.7 to 0.95 and watch the KV block count move. Understand that this is the weights-versus-cache split, not a safety margin.
Change `--max-num-seqs` and `--max-num-batched-tokens` and observe the effect on the reported concurrency and on a small burst of requests.
Point the official `openai` Python client at your endpoint with a dummy API key, and confirm both streaming and non-streaming completions work — Phase 3 depends on exactly this.
Save the working command line in your repo as a script. You will re-run it a dozen times over the next three weeks.

Continuous batching and paged KV cache.desc: Static batching idles the GPU whenever sequences finish at different times; continuous batching admits new requests at every decode step. PagedAttention is what makes that admission cheap — fixed-size KV blocks plus an indirection table, so there is no contiguous per-sequence reservation to fragment. Preemption under memory pressure is a real behaviour, not a footnote.
steps: Read the paged-attention design doc and draw the block table for two sequences: logical KV positions on one side, physical block IDs on the other.
Work out the memory waste of the naive alternative — contiguous allocation sized to `max_model_len` — for a workload whose actual outputs are short. The ratio is the whole argument for paging.
Read how blocks are allocated, shared (copy-on-write for forked sequences) and evicted, and identify what triggers preemption.
Force preemption: lower `--gpu-memory-utilization` and fire more concurrent long-output requests than the cache can hold. Find the preemption warning in the logs and watch throughput collapse.
Explain in writing why continuous batching needs paging to be practical — admitting a request mid-flight is only cheap if you can hand it blocks without moving anyone else's cache.
Note the two knobs that control this in practice (`--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-num-seqs`) and what each one does to the failure you just produced.

Read the PagedAttention paper.desc: The original vLLM paper is short and states the problem cleanly: for LLM serving it is KV cache memory, not compute, that bounds throughput, and pre-allocating contiguous cache for the maximum sequence length wastes most of it. The framing and the memory accounting carry over to every serving system built since.
steps: Read the paper start to finish in one sitting — it is short — and write the thesis in one sentence before looking at any commentary.
Reproduce the memory-waste taxonomy in your own words: internal fragmentation, external fragmentation, and reservation for future tokens. Estimate each for your own serving config.

Note the sharing mechanisms the paper introduces — shared prefixes for parallel sampling and beam search via copy-on-write blocks — because that is the direct ancestor of prefix caching two items from now.
Read the evaluation section critically: what baselines, what workloads, and which of its claimed speedups depend on the output-length distribution rather than on paging itself.
Read the Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference paper alongside it for the complementary view — the arithmetic of latency versus throughput on sharded hardware.
Write half a page connecting the paper's accounting to the KV block count your own server reported at startup.

Prefix caching.desc: Automatic prefix caching hashes KV blocks so requests sharing a prefix reuse them instead of recomputing. For eval and RL workloads — hundreds of samples behind one long system prompt and few-shot block — this is the single largest win available, and it is a number worth measuring rather than quoting.
steps: Read the design doc and understand the hashing scheme: blocks are keyed on the hash of their token contents plus the hash of the preceding block, which is what makes reuse safe across requests.
Build a synthetic eval batch that mirrors your Phase 3 workload — one long shared system prompt and few-shot block, then a short per-sample suffix.
Run it with prefix caching disabled and record time-to-first-token distribution and total throughput.
Run the identical batch with prefix caching enabled and record the same two metrics. Compute the speedup and note that it lands almost entirely in TTFT, not in decode.
Check the cache hit rate the engine reports and confirm it matches your expectation from the prompt structure. A low hit rate usually means your prefix is not byte-identical across requests.
Sweep the shared-prefix length and plot speedup against it, then write down the prefix length below which caching stops mattering for your workload.

Tensor-parallel and multi-GPU serving.desc: Serving a model too large for one card means `--tensor-parallel-size`. TP splits both the weights and the KV cache, so you get cache headroom as well as compute — but you also pay an all-reduce per layer, so latency improves sub-linearly and per-GPU throughput usually goes down. Measure per-GPU, not aggregate.
steps: Serve the same model at TP=1 and at TP=2 and record the KV block count each reports at startup. The increase is the cache headroom TP buys you.
Run an identical load at both settings and record tokens/second, then divide by the GPU count. Compare tokens/second per GPU, which is the number that tells you whether TP paid for itself.
Measure inter-token latency at low concurrency in both configurations — this is where TP should genuinely win, because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound.

Read the parallelism doc on when to prefer pipeline parallel (across nodes, where the interconnect is slow) versus tensor parallel (within a node over NVLink), and relate it to the fabric numbers from scaling-book chapter 12.
Deliberately break it: request a TP size that does not divide the attention head count, and read the error so you recognise it later.
Read the distributed-troubleshooting page and note the two or three environment variables it tells you to set when a multi-GPU server hangs at startup.

Throughput versus latency, measured.desc: There is one curve every serving engineer should be able to draw from memory: throughput rises with concurrency until the KV cache saturates and then flattens or collapses, while per-request latency degrades from the very first concurrent request. Find the knee on your own endpoint, because Phase 3's eval runs will sit right on it.
steps: Use vLLM's benchmark CLI first to get a trustworthy baseline before writing anything yourself — it already handles warmup and percentile reporting correctly.
Then write your own small async load generator so you control the request shape: fixed input length, fixed output length, and a concurrency parameter.
Sweep concurrency across at least six points and record, at each: time-to-first-token (p50 and p95), inter-token latency, and total output tokens/second.
Plot throughput against concurrency and latency against concurrency on the same x-axis. Mark the knee, and cross-check it against the maximum concurrency the engine reported at startup.
Push past the knee until you see preemption in the logs, and note what happens to p95 TTFT when it fires.
Repeat the sweep with a long-input/short-output shape and a short-input/long-output shape, and note that the knee moves. Record the operating point you will actually use in Phase 3.

Quantization.desc: Quantization is the cheapest way to fit a bigger model or a bigger KV cache on the hardware you already rent. The distinctions that matter in practice are weight-only versus weight-and-activation, FP8 versus INT8 versus 4-bit, and — separately from all of that — whether you quantize the KV cache. The accuracy cost is workload-dependent, so measure yours.
steps: Read the quantization index and write down which schemes your GPU actually supports in hardware; FP8 on pre-Hopper cards is emulated and will not give you the speedup you expect.
Serve one model at bf16 and the same model at FP8 W8A8, and record tokens/second, KV block count and peak memory for each.

Separately enable KV cache quantization (FP8 KV) at bf16 weights, and record the increase in KV blocks. Note that this is an independent decision from weight quantization and often the better one for long-context eval workloads.
Try one 4-bit weight-only scheme and note where it wins (memory-bound single-stream decode) and where it loses (compute-bound large-batch prefill).

Evaluate all the configurations you served on the same task with the same prompts, and record the accuracy delta alongside the throughput delta. A throughput number without an accuracy number is not a result.
Write a short recommendation for your own Phase 3 workload with the measured numbers attached, and say explicitly which configuration you rejected and why.

Speculative decoding.desc: A draft model, an n-gram lookup or a self-speculation head proposes several tokens; the target model verifies them in a single forward pass and accepts the longest correct prefix. The output distribution is provably unchanged, so it is a pure latency win — but only at high acceptance and small batch. On a throughput-bound eval run it can make things worse.
steps: Read one of the two original papers far enough to convince yourself of the correctness argument: modified rejection sampling makes the output distribution identical to plain sampling from the target.
Enable n-gram (prompt-lookup) speculation first, since it needs no second model, and measure inter-token latency at concurrency 1 against your baseline.
Enable a real draft model and measure both acceptance rate and end-to-end latency. Acceptance rate is the number that predicts whether it will help.
Now re-run the same configuration at high concurrency and show that the benefit shrinks or inverts, because verification FLOPs compete with the batch you are already running.
Vary the number of speculative tokens and find the optimum for your workload — more proposals help only until the acceptance probability of the last one gets small.
Write the decision rule you will apply in Phase 3: on for interactive single-stream work, off for throughput-bound batch eval, with your measured numbers as evidence.

SGLang and structured generation.desc: SGLang is the other serving engine you should be able to speak to. Its distinguishing pieces are RadixAttention — a prefix tree over the KV cache that generalises prefix caching to arbitrary shared prefixes, which is exactly what branching agent traces produce — and fast constrained decoding for JSON and grammar-bounded output.
steps: Read the SGLang paper for RadixAttention and the LRU eviction policy over the radix tree, and articulate how it differs from vLLM's block-hash prefix caching for a branching workload.
Install SGLang and serve the same model you used on vLLM, then hit its OpenAI-compatible endpoint to confirm the client code is unchanged.
Run your own load generator against SGLang at the same concurrency sweep and compare the throughput and latency curves against your vLLM numbers directly.
Build a branching workload — one shared prompt, several divergent continuations, then further branches — and compare both engines on it. This is where RadixAttention should show its advantage.
Use SGLang's structured outputs to force a JSON schema and then a small grammar, and measure the latency cost of constrained decoding versus free generation.
Write the comparison: which engine you would pick for an agentic eval workload, the measured evidence, and the one thing that would change your mind. That writeup is a milestone deliverable.

Wire the endpoint to an RL and eval harn.desc: Close the loop that motivates the whole task. Prime Intellect's `verifiers` assumes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint backed by vLLM, so point it at the server you just built and run one trivial rollout. You are not learning the library yet — that comes in week 25 — you are proving the plumbing and finding where the endpoint becomes the bottleneck.
steps: Install `verifiers` and read its overview far enough to know what it expects: a base URL, an API key it will not check, and a model name that matches what your server reports at `/v1/models`.
Point it at your running vLLM server and execute the smallest built-in environment you can find. Success is a completed rollout, not a good score.
Turn the concurrency up until the rollout loop stops getting faster, and confirm from the server logs that the endpoint — not the harness — is the limiter.
Turn prefix caching on and re-run; a rollout loop with a fixed system prompt should show exactly the TTFT win you measured earlier.
Repeat the same trivial rollout against your SGLang server to prove the harness really is engine-agnostic, and note anything that had to change.

Write down the endpoint configuration you will standardise on for the rest of this phase — model, TP size, max-model-len, prefix caching, quantization — with the measurement that justifies each choice.

Decide the sample size before you run an.desc: Power analysis is the reflex that separates an eval engineer from someone running a script. Before any comparison, work out what difference n questions could even detect — and discover how brutal n = 100 really is.
steps: Write the comparison down first: two models on one benchmark (independent-ish), or one model before/after a change (paired). The design decides the test.
Use `statsmodels.stats.power.NormalIndPower().solve_power()` with `proportion_effectsize(p1, p2)` to get the minimum detectable effect at 80% power for n = 100, 500, 2000.
Tabulate MDE against n and stare at it: at n = 100 you typically cannot resolve anything under ~10 accuracy points. Save that table in your stats notebook.
Redo it for the paired case with `TTestPower` — the paired design usually buys you a 2–4x smaller n for the same MDE. That is the whole argument for scoring both models on the same questions.
Add a `plan_eval(n, baseline_acc, target_delta)` helper to your notebook that refuses (raises) when the requested delta is below the MDE.
Apply it once for real: pick an eval you were about to run and either enlarge n or narrow the claim you intend to make.

Read the error-bars paper and apply it t.desc: Anthropic's "Adding Error Bars to Evals" is the single most reusable eval paper there is: standard error over questions, the clustered case, and the paired analysis that makes model comparisons far tighter. Read it, then recompute error bars on a result you already published.

Implement `mean_and_se(scores)` for the simple case, and check it against the closed form for a Bernoulli mean: `sqrt(p(1-p)/n)`.

Write the CI into your results format so every number your harness emits carries `mean`, `se`, `n`, and `n_clusters`.
Read Anthropic's companion blog post for the plain-language version you can reuse in an interview answer.

Paired comparison and variance decomposi.desc: Two models scored on the same questions are paired data. Analysing them as independent samples throws away most of your power. Then decompose the remaining variance — question difficulty, decoding temperature, seed — and find out which one you should actually be buying more of.
steps: Score both models on the identical question set, keep per-question results, and run `scipy.stats.ttest_rel` on the per-question difference; compare the interval width against the unpaired `ttest_ind`.
Add the non-parametric fallback (`scipy.stats.wilcoxon`) for the case where the per-question difference is far from normal.
Bootstrap the paired difference with `scipy.stats.bootstrap(..., paired=True)` and report the CI on the difference, not two overlapping CIs on two means.
Decompose variance: fix questions and resample seeds (decoding variance), then fix seeds and resample questions (question variance). Report both numbers separately.
State the conclusion explicitly: if question variance dominates, more questions beat more samples per question — and that is a budget decision, not a statistics footnote.
Add both tests to the stats notebook with a docstring saying when each applies.

Multiple comparisons and effect sizes.desc: Run twelve ablations against one baseline and one of them is significant by accident. Implement Benjamini–Hochberg and Bonferroni, see what survives, and then stop leading with p-values — report the effect size with a bootstrap interval instead.
steps: Simulate the problem first: generate 12 null comparisons (no real effect) and count how often at least one p < 0.05. Seeing ~46% makes the correction non-negotiable.
Apply `statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests` with `method='bonferroni'` and `method='fdr_bh'` to a real family of ablations and record which survive each.
Understand the difference you are choosing between: family-wise error rate (Bonferroni, conservative) versus false discovery rate (BH, what you usually want for screening).
Rewrite your results table so the headline column is the effect size with a bootstrap CI, and the p-value is a secondary column.
Pre-register the comparison family in the notebook: which comparisons you intend to make, before you look at the numbers. Post-hoc family size is how people cheat themselves.
Write one sentence per surviving result distinguishing 'small but real' from 'large but uncertain'.

Exit check: redo an old result honestly.desc: Take the single-variable change you measured back in the nanochat week and redo the analysis properly — paired where possible, bootstrap CI, stated n, stated seeds. Then publish whether it survives. A public correction is worth more in an interview than the original claim.
steps: Pull the raw per-sample outputs of the old result. If you did not keep them, that is finding number one — write it down and fix the harness so it never happens again.
Re-run the analysis paired on the same questions, with a bootstrap CI on the difference and an explicit n, seed list, and decode configuration.
Check whether the original comparison was part of a larger family; if so, apply BH correction across that family.
Write the paragraph: what you claimed, what the honest interval is, and whether the claim survives. Publish it in the same place the original went.
Turn the whole thing into a reusable `analysis.ipynb` with functions — power, paired test, bootstrap CI, multiple-comparison correction — that every later task in this phase imports.
Add a results-schema check: any number your harness emits without n, seeds, and a CI should fail validation.

The loop, from a blank file.desc: No framework. Write the while loop yourself: send messages, parse the tool call, dispatch to a Python function, append the tool result, repeat until the model stops or you hit a limit. Two hundred lines, and afterwards every agent framework reads as a config file rather than magic.
steps: Start from a bare `messages` list and one tool. Call the model, check `stop_reason`, and branch: if it asked for a tool, execute and append a tool-result block; otherwise return.
Write the dispatch table as a plain `dict[str, Callable]` — no registry, no decorators. You want the control flow visible on one screen.
Make the loop async from the start so Phase 0's `asyncio.gather` / semaphore patterns apply directly when you run many tasks at once.
Log every turn to a JSONL trajectory file: request messages, raw response, tool name, tool args, tool result, latency, tokens. This file is the product.
Read Anthropic's "Building effective agents" and mark which of its patterns (prompt chaining, routing, evaluator-optimiser) your loop already covers for free.
Then read Inspect's ReAct agent source and diff the shape against yours — same loop, plus submit tooling, limits, and message trimming.

Tool schema design is the actual skill.desc: Write five tools, then rewrite them. Names and descriptions are prompt, not documentation — the model fails on ambiguous parameters far more often than on hard reasoning. Return errors as content the model can act on, and keep outputs small enough that ten calls do not blow the context.
steps: Write five tools with real work behind them: a file reader, a shell runner, a search, a structured-data query, and one domain tool for your Phase 3 environment.
Rewrite every description as instruction to the model, not to a human: state when to use it, when not to, and what the parameters mean in the model's terms. Include one worked example per tool.
Kill ambiguous parameters — no bare `query: str` where a path was meant, no optional flags whose default the model cannot infer. Use enums and required fields aggressively.
Convert exceptions into tool-result content: `{"error": "path not found", "hint": "list the directory first"}`. An exception ends the run; an error message lets the model recover.
Cap every tool's output (head/tail plus a truncation marker with an identifier the model can use to fetch more) and measure token cost per call.
A/B it: run the same 20 tasks with the first draft and the rewrite, and report the success-rate delta with a paired CI from Task 01.

Multi-turn state, error recovery, hard l.desc: Add the things that keep a harness alive over 50 turns: bounded concurrency, retries with backoff, a step limit, a wall-clock limit, and a cost cap that aborts the run. Then deliberately break a tool and watch whether your agent loops forever — most first drafts do.
steps: Wrap the model call in retry-with-jittered-backoff for 429/5xx/timeouts only. Never retry a 400 — that is your bug, and retrying hides it.
Add four independent limits: max steps, max wall-clock, max total tokens, max dollars. Each raises a distinct typed exception so the trajectory records *which* limit ended the run.
Bound concurrency with an `asyncio.Semaphore` sized to your rate limit, and make the cost cap process-global rather than per-task.
Break a tool on purpose — make it always return the same error — and confirm the loop terminates. Add a repeated-identical-failure detector if it does not.
Distinguish a *sample error* (this task failed) from a *harness error* (the run is invalid) in your logs; conflating them is how flaky infrastructure becomes a capability claim.
Read Inspect's Setting Limits and Handling Errors pages and copy the taxonomy rather than inventing your own.

Context compaction.desc: Long agentic runs die from context, not capability. Implement one strategy and measure it — summarise older turns, drop stale tool outputs while keeping their identifiers, or offload results to files the agent can re-read. Compare success with and without on the same tasks so you end up with a number, not a preference.
steps: Instrument first: plot context length per turn across your longest runs and find where the failures cluster. Compaction without that plot is guesswork.
Implement one strategy end to end. The cheapest that works is usually tool-output eviction: replace old outputs with a stub plus a handle the agent can re-read on demand.
Then implement summarisation as the comparison arm: when context crosses a threshold, summarise the oldest k turns into a single message and keep the system prompt and the task statement verbatim.
Guard the invariant that breaks everything: never drop the message that contains the current sub-goal, and never orphan a tool_use block from its tool_result.
Run the same task set with and without compaction, report paired success-rate difference with a CI, and report tokens saved per task alongside it.

Build a server with the official Python SDK exposing two of your tools plus one resource; run it over stdio first because it is the easiest to debug.
Add a client path to your own harness: launch the server, negotiate, list tools, and merge them into the same dispatch table your native tools use.

LoRA from scratch — it is two matrices a.desc: Implement a LoRA layer in PyTorch: A initialised Gaussian, B initialised to zero, output scaled by alpha over r. Inject it into your Phase 1 transformer, verify the trainable parameter count drops by the factor you predicted, confirm gradients flow only into A and B, and merge the adapter back into the base weights.
steps: Write `LoRALinear(base: nn.Linear, r: int, alpha: float)` that freezes `base.weight`, adds `A` (r × in, Gaussian) and `B` (out × r, zeros), and returns `base(x) + (alpha/r) * (x @ A.T @ B.T)`.
Prove B=0 matters: assert the wrapped module's output equals the base module's output exactly at initialisation. If it does not, your merge will be wrong too.
Inject into q_proj and v_proj of your Phase 1 transformer, then compute `trainable/total` and check it against the number you predicted from r, alpha, and the injected shapes.
Run one backward pass and assert `base.weight.grad is None` while `A.grad` and `B.grad` are populated — that is the actual PEFT invariant.
Implement `merge()` that folds `(alpha/r) * B @ A` into `base.weight`, and assert merged-model outputs match unmerged within float tolerance.
Sweep r ∈ {1, 4, 16, 64} on a tiny task and plot quality against trainable parameters so you have your own version of the paper's rank ablation.

Configure `SFTTrainer` with a `LoraConfig` from peft, and check `print_trainable_parameters()` against the prediction you made in the from-scratch task.
Turn on completion-only loss (mask the prompt) and confirm it is actually applied — training on the prompt is the most common silent SFT bug.

Dataset card and leakage check.desc: Write the dataset card before you publish the adapter — provenance, licence, size, splits, known limitations. Then actually check for train/eval contamination with exact-match and near-duplicate search between your training set and whatever you plan to evaluate on. Report the overlap number even when it is zero.
steps: Write the card from the Hub template first: source, collection method, licence, size, split definition, intended use, and known limitations. Doing it before the run changes what you collect.
Run exact-match contamination: normalise whitespace and case, hash every training example and every eval question, and report the intersection size.
Run near-duplicate contamination: n-gram overlap (13-gram is the common convention) or MinHash/LSH, with a stated threshold. Report the count and show the top ten matches by hand.
Check the base model too — you cannot fix pretraining contamination, but you can say which benchmarks are compromised for the model you chose and cite the leakage literature.
Publish the overlap number in the card as a first-class field, including when it is zero, plus the exact script that produced it.
Add the check to CI so the number is recomputed whenever the training set changes.

Run a GRPO-family loop on a verifiable t.desc: Use TRL's GRPO trainer on something with a programmatic checker — arithmetic with hidden state, or a format-plus-answer task. TRL v1.9.0 flipped the default `loss_type` to "dapo" and marks plain `grpo` as not recommended because of length bias. Read what that default is doing before you accept it, and log reward curves rather than only final accuracy.
steps: Write the checker first, as a pure function with unit tests. If you cannot write the reward as code you do not have a verifiable task.
Use two reward functions, not one: a format reward and a correctness reward, logged separately — the first almost always saturates before the second moves.
Read the `loss_type` section of the GRPOTrainer docs and write down in your own words what `dapo` changes versus `grpo` (token-level normalisation) before you keep the default.
Stand up an OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint for generation; on-policy sampling throughput, not gradient steps, is what bounds this run.
Log per-step: mean reward, reward std within group, completion length, KL to reference, and fraction of groups with zero advantage (all-correct or all-wrong groups contribute nothing).
Report the honest outcome: reward curve versus held-out eval, with the paired CI from Task 01. Reward going up while eval does not is the interesting result, not a failure.

Know where GRPO and DAPO came from.desc: GRPO is introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper: drop the value model, normalise advantage within a sampled group. DAPO then fixes four concrete failures — clip-higher, dynamic sampling, token-level loss, overlong-reward shaping — and that token-level loss is exactly the length-bias fix behind TRL's new default. Read both and you can explain your config line by line.
steps: Read DeepSeekMath (arXiv 2402.03300) §4 and derive the GRPO objective yourself from PPO by replacing the learned value baseline with the within-group mean.

Read DAPO (arXiv 2503.14476) and write one paragraph per fix: clip-higher (entropy collapse), dynamic sampling (zero-gradient groups), token-level loss (length bias), overlong reward shaping (truncation noise).
Map each fix onto a TRL config field and note which ones TRL exposes and which it does not.
Read DeepSeek-R1 (arXiv 2501.12948) for the part most people skip: they dropped process reward models for rule-based outcome rewards. Know why before someone asks.
Skim the PPO paper for the clipped surrogate objective so you can say precisely what GRPO kept and what it threw away.

Read the RLVR capability debate honestly.desc: This is contested ground and knowing that is the point. Read 2504.13837 (base models win at large k), 2506.10947 (Spurious Rewards — random rewards help Qwen but not Llama or OLMo), 2505.24864 (ProRL — prolonged RL does expand the boundary), then 2510.04028, which reconciles them: early training exploits and narrows, prolonged training explores and expands.
steps: Read 2504.13837 first and get precise about pass@k: at k=1 RL wins, at large k the base model catches up. The claim is about the *support* of the distribution, not the mean.
Read Spurious Rewards (2506.10947) and note the load-bearing detail: the effect appears on Qwen and not on Llama or OLMo. Any RLVR result on a single model family is a result about that family.
Read ProRL (2505.24864) as the rebuttal — enough steps, enough task diversity, and the boundary does move.
Read the two-stage reconciliation (2510.04028) last and write the synthesis: the camps measured different phases of the same curve.
Test one claim on your own run: compute pass@1 and pass@k for base and RL'd model on your verifiable task and see which side your data lands on.

Learn what actually moves the number.desc: "The Art of Scaling RL Compute" spends 400k+ GPU-hours and finds sigmoidal rather than power-law curves: design choices buy compute efficiency, they do not raise the asymptote. The practical lesson is to stop collecting GRPO variants — pick one, scale it as far as your budget goes, and measure the curve you get.
steps: Read 2510.13786 and extract the two parameters that matter: the asymptote (what the recipe can ever reach) and the efficiency (how fast it gets there). Most published wins move the second.
Fit the same shape to your own run: plot held-out score against cumulative training compute, not against steps, and try a sigmoid fit rather than a line.
Freeze your recipe. Spend the remaining budget on one long run instead of five short ablations — the paper's whole point is that short runs mispredict.
Pair it with the two-stage RLVR paper: an early-phase measurement of your own run will look like narrowing, and that is expected rather than a bug.

Write the budget conclusion: given your compute, what is the largest claim your curve supports?

steps: Read the reward-modelling chapter and implement a tiny Bradley–Terry reward model on a preference set so the loss is not abstract.

Read the regularisation chapter and sweep the KL coefficient on your own run — watch reward go up and coherence go down.

Train against your own environment.desc: Point a trainer at your environment to find out whether the interface actually holds. A bad learning curve is a fine outcome; a broken reset is the finding.
steps: Run a short GRPO job against your environment using the setup from earlier this week.
Watch for state leaking between episodes — the most common defect in a first environment.
Check whether the reward is dense enough to learn from, and note what it fails to credit.
Record wall-clock and cost per rollout; RL amplifies both far beyond eval usage.
Write the defects into the week-38 backlog rather than fixing them now.

A job queue over checkpoints.desc: Build the thing the job req lists first: submit (model, task, sample) jobs to a persistent queue, run them with bounded concurrency, retry transient failures with backoff, and resume cleanly after you kill the process halfway through. Idempotent job keys are the whole design — get them right and everything else is bookkeeping.
steps: Define the job key before anything else: a hash over model id, task id, sample id, epoch, decode parameters, and harness version. Same key means same work, forever.

Persist state in SQLite with a `UNIQUE` constraint on the job key and an explicit status column (`pending / running / done / failed / abandoned`). The database is the queue; do not hold state in memory.
Run with bounded concurrency (`asyncio.Semaphore`), commit each result transactionally, and make submission idempotent so re-submitting the same sweep is a no-op.
Write the crash test as a real test: launch 500 jobs, `kill -9` the process at ~40%, restart, and assert total completions equal 500 with zero duplicates.
Handle the leased-job problem: a `running` row whose worker died must time out back to `pending`, or your queue stalls silently.
Study Inspect's eval-set model — task/epoch identity, log-driven resume — before you invent your own resume semantics.

Caching and dedupe that you can trust.desc: Cache completed samples keyed on model id, prompt, decode parameters, and harness version. Deduplicate identical work inside a batch. Then test the failure mode deliberately: change a prompt template and confirm the cache misses instead of silently serving last week's answers.
steps: Make the cache key explicit and total: model id *and* version string, full rendered prompt, temperature/top_p/max_tokens/seed, tool set, and a harness version you bump by hand.
Read Inspect's caching page and copy its scoping decisions rather than inventing them — especially what it does *not* include in the key.
Add in-batch dedupe: collapse identical (prompt, params) requests to a single call and fan the result back out, then log how many calls that saved.
Write the invalidation test: change one character of the prompt template, re-run, and assert a cache miss. Then bump the harness version and assert a miss again. This test is the deliverable.
Give cache entries a TTL and record the timestamp and model version in the entry, so a stale hit is at least attributable.
Add a `--no-cache` flag and a report line showing hit rate and dollars saved per run.

Sandbox the agentic tasks.desc: Agentic evals run untrusted model-generated code. Each sample gets a container with no network by default, an explicit allowlist when a task needs one, CPU and memory limits, a timeout, and guaranteed cleanup even when the run crashes. Inspect's sandbox model is the reference implementation to copy rather than reinvent.
steps: Default to `--network none` and make network access an explicit, per-task opt-in that is recorded in the sample log. A task that quietly reaches the internet is not reproducible.
Set hard resource limits: `--memory`, `--cpus`, `--pids-limit`, and a read-only root filesystem with a single writable scratch mount.
Enforce a per-sample timeout outside the container, and guarantee teardown with `try/finally` plus a reaper pass that removes orphaned containers on startup.
Read Inspect's sandboxing docs and the sandbox-extension API, then decide whether to implement its interface directly so your environment is portable.
Escalate the isolation story where it matters: know when a gVisor-style runtime or a remote sandbox provider is the right answer versus plain Docker.
Test the sandbox adversarially: a task that tries to write outside scratch, one that forks bombs, one that curls an external host. All three must fail closed and be logged.

Per-sample cost and token accounting.desc: Record input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, tool calls, wall-clock, and dollar cost for every sample — not per run, per sample. That is how you answer "what would this eval cost on the next model" without guessing, and how you find the one task eating 40% of your budget.
steps: Extract usage from every API response — input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens — and store it on the sample row, not aggregated.
Keep a versioned price table keyed by model id and date; compute cost at write time and store both the cost and the price-table version so old numbers stay reproducible.
Add per-sample wall-clock, model-call count, tool-call count, and retry count. Retry count is how you discover that 5% of samples are burning 30% of spend.
Build the two queries that matter: cost per task (find the expensive task) and cost per completed sample (find the flaky task), then rank both.
Implement projection: `estimate_cost(task, model, n)` from historical per-sample medians, and check it against a real run before you trust it.
Wire it to the cost cap from Task 02 so the queue aborts a sweep rather than discovering the overrun on the invoice.

A dashboard someone else can read.desc: Ship a view showing score per task per checkpoint with the confidence intervals from Task 01, run status and failure counts, cost to date, and a link from any number to the raw sample logs behind it. Plot intervals, never bare bars. Reuse the CI helpers from Task 01 so the dashboard and the notebook can never disagree.

Label the gold set yourself first.desc: Hand-label at least 100 samples before the judge sees them, writing down the decision rule as you go. Then measure judge–human agreement properly: raw agreement, Cohen's kappa, and a per-class breakdown — because a judge that is 90% accurate overall can be useless on the 10% of cases you actually care about.
steps: Sample 100+ items *stratified* over the outcomes you care about, not uniformly. A gold set with three failures in it cannot measure failure detection.
Label them yourself before writing the judge prompt, and write the decision rule down as you go — every time you hesitate, that hesitation is a rubric line you owe the judge.
Re-label 20 of them a week later and compute your own self-agreement. That number is the ceiling on any judge you build; report it.
Compute raw agreement, Cohen's kappa (`sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score`), and the full confusion matrix — kappa alone hides which class is failing.
Add the confidence interval: bootstrap agreement over the 100 samples with the Task 01 machinery and report the interval, not the point estimate.
Commit the gold set and labels to the repo as data, with the decision rule as a markdown file next to it.

Run the bias battery.desc: Test the known failure modes on your own judge: position bias (swap A and B, measure how often the verdict flips), length bias (pad a response without adding content), and self-preference. The MT-Bench paper is where these were characterised and it gives you the experimental designs to copy.
steps: Position bias: run every pairwise comparison in both orders and report the flip rate. Anything above a few percent means you must always evaluate both orders and average.
Length bias: pad the losing response with on-topic but contentless filler at 1.2x, 1.5x, 2x length and plot win rate against length ratio.
Self-preference: have judge model A grade outputs from A and from B on items where your human labels say they are equal, and report the gap.
Add a sanity arm the field keeps rediscovering — a degenerate constant response — and confirm your judge does not reward it.
Report each bias as an effect size with a bootstrap CI, not a single anecdote, and correct across the battery with Benjamini–Hochberg from Task 01.
Fix what you can in the prompt (order randomisation, explicit length-neutrality instruction, reference-guided grading) and re-measure — the delta is your result.

Rubrics and checklists, not scalar score.desc: In non-verifiable domains, explicit criteria beat learned reward models — see Rubrics as Rewards (2507.17746) and Checklists Are Better Than Reward Models (2507.18624). steps: Read the two 2025 rubric papers and HealthBench, and note the common structure: per-item criteria attached to the specific conversation, not a global scale.
Take your worst-performing judge prompt and decompose its scalar score into 5–10 binary checklist items, each independently checkable.
Score the checklist items separately and aggregate in code, not in the model. Aggregation in the prompt is where scalar judges lose their calibration.
Re-run the gold set and report the agreement delta with a CI. Also report which individual items the judge gets wrong — that is where the rubric is ambiguous, not where the model is dumb.
Write the rubric so a second human can apply it, then have someone apply it. Inter-rater agreement on the rubric bounds what the judge can achieve.
Wire the checklist into a custom scorer so the per-item results land in the sample log, not just the aggregate.

Calibration drift and version pinning.desc: A judge is a model and it changes under you. Pin the exact judge model version in results, keep the gold set in the repo, and re-run it whenever the judge model, its prompt, or its decode parameters change. steps: Pin the judge to a dated model id — never an alias like `-latest`. Store the resolved id in every result row.
Treat the judge prompt as versioned code: hash it into the result and into the cache key from Task 05, so a prompt edit invalidates cached grades.
Set judge decode parameters explicitly (temperature 0 or a fixed seed) and record them; a judge sampled at default temperature is a different judge every run.
Build `judge_regression.py`: re-run the gold set, compute agreement plus CI, and fail if it drops more than a stated threshold from the recorded baseline.
Keep an agreement-per-version table in the repo. When a score moves, the first question is always 'did the judge move?' — this table answers it in seconds.
Run the regression on a schedule, not only on change: providers update models under stable-looking names.

Read the protocol before you read the nu.desc: Write down what the benchmark's own rules say: step limits, retries and pass@k, allowed tools, scaffold constraints, model version, and which splits count. τ²-bench is a good one to study because its dual-control setup makes the protocol assumptions explicit rather than implicit. steps: Build a protocol checklist as a YAML file with one row per rule: step limit, agent timeout, test timeout, trials per task, dataset version, allowed tools, allowed scaffold modifications, scoring rule.

Read the τ²-bench paper for how a well-specified protocol reads: dual control means the user simulator's abilities are part of the spec, and that is normally left implicit.
Note every rule that is enforced by code versus by honour. The honour-system rules are exactly where published results drift.
Read the Harbor docs for how the official harness sets timeouts and concurrency, and record the defaults you inherit.

Fix the free variables to the published values: model id, temperature, step limit, trials per task, dataset version. Record every value you had to guess.
Pick your coverage honestly: a stratified random subset with a stated n and a CI beats a cherry-picked easy subset. Compute the MDE for your n from Task 01 before you start.
Run at least the benchmark's minimum trials per task — single-trial agentic numbers are dominated by run-to-run variance.
Persist everything: full trajectories, per-sample cost, container exit codes, and which limit terminated each run. Publish the logs alongside the report.
Track your own environment failure rate separately from task failure. If 8% of your samples crashed, your number is not comparable to anyone's.

Report the discrepancy.desc: Write your number against the published one with confidence intervals, and separate the explanations: protocol deviation, scaffold difference, model version drift, or genuine irreproducibility. Check the submitted result JSON for protocol-compliance flags — published results have shipped with raised step limits and `followed_evaluation_protocol` set to "No". Then file an issue with the maintainers.
steps: Put both numbers on one plot with intervals. If the intervals overlap, the honest headline is 'consistent within uncertainty', however disappointing that is.
Open the submitted result JSON and check the compliance metadata directly — step limits, timeouts, trial counts, and any protocol-compliance flag. Quote the field rather than paraphrasing it.
Attribute the gap across four buckets with evidence for each: protocol deviation, scaffold difference, model version drift, genuine irreproducibility. Say which you could not distinguish.
State your own limitations first and prominently: coverage, n, trials, budget, and anything you had to guess.
Contact the maintainers privately before publishing, give them time to respond, and include their reply. Then file the public issue.
Publish the report with the raw logs and the exact commands. The reproducibility of your audit is the whole point of the audit.

WebVoyager never had a leaderboard at all. AssistantBench and WebGames are still cited long past usefulness, and the original τ-bench repo is deprecated with README numbers roughly eighteen months stale. steps: Read the original papers for WebArena, WebVoyager, AssistantBench and τ-bench — enough to state what each actually measured and what its headline number was at publication.
Check each one's current state yourself: is there a maintained leaderboard, when did the repo last move, and are the README numbers current? Screenshot the evidence.
Classify each as saturated (near human baseline), unmaintained, never-had-a-leaderboard, or superseded — these are different diseases with different symptoms.
Trace one citation chain: find a 2026 paper citing a dead benchmark's numbers and follow it back to where the number came from. That is the mechanism of persistence.
Read the leaderboard-illusion and can-we-trust-benchmarks papers for the structural reasons, not just the anecdotes.
Write the survey section: three benchmarks, why each is dead, why it is still cited, and what to use instead.

Learn where computer-use numbers hide.desc: Computer-use benchmarks concentrate every way an agent number can mislead, which makes them the best place to learn to read one. The score column is the least informative part of the table.
steps: Download the OSWorld-Verified results spreadsheet and sort by model rather than by score — the site renders it via JavaScript, so parse the xlsx directly.
Find the same model at different `Max steps` values and note the spread: one Sonnet release runs 42.9 / 58.1 / 62.9% at 15 / 50 / 100 steps, and at least one model scores worse with more steps.
Check the `Multiple rollout` flag before believing any headline. A widely-quoted 'above human baseline' result was ten rollouts plus a judge, reported next to pass@1 numbers.

Compare a lab's self-reported figure against the maintainer's verified table for the same benchmark — a ~12-point gap on the same benchmark name is normal when the harness differs, and labs retroactively restate old scores when they change harnesses.

Read the OSWorld-Verified postmortem for what rots in a live environment: sites changing HTML, CAPTCHAs, booking tasks that expire as dates pass, over-strict evaluators needing colour tolerance and fuzzy matching.
Write down, for your chosen benchmark, every free parameter a submitter could vary without lying.

Measure what a single number hides.desc: Rerun, report the spread, and price the run. Accuracy without variance and without cost per solved task is a marketing number, not a measurement.
steps: Run your chosen task subset at three to five seeds and report per-task success variance, not just the mean.
Separate the sources of variation you can see: execution stochasticity, ambiguous task specifications, and genuine behavioural variability.

Record cost per task and cost per solved task alongside accuracy — at frontier prices a 108-task computer-use run is thousands of dollars, and on GAIA the top agent costs roughly 23x a cheap model for 42 points.
State your own step budget, harness version, and rollout count in the report, in the terms you wished the original submission had used.
If your reproduction agrees with the published number, say so plainly — a confirmed result is still a result, and it is evidence you can be trusted with the ones that do not agree.

Audit your own environment the same way.desc: Apply the audit lens to yourself and publish what it finds. Pre-empting the criticism is worth more than surviving it.
steps: Write down every parameter someone could vary without lying: step budget, retries, temperature, harness version, rollout count.
Ask whether a submitter could inflate a score by changing something you never documented, then document it.
If you quote a human baseline, state how it was constructed, by how many people, under what time limit.
Check your verifier for false negatives on correct-but-unusual answers.
Publish all of it as a limitations section rather than a footnote.

Read one frontier safety framework prope.desc: Read Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy end to end, then skim Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework for contrast. Learn the vocabulary that structures the whole field: capability thresholds, safety cases, evaluation triggers, and what it means for a model to be deployed under a specific safety level.
steps: Read the RSP straight through and build a glossary as you go: capability threshold, required safeguards, ASL, evaluation trigger, safety case, iterative commitment.

Read DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework v3 next and diff the vocabulary — critical capability levels versus ASLs, alert thresholds versus evaluation triggers. The mapping is not one-to-one and interviewers ask about the gap.
Read the ASL-3 activation announcement for the concrete case: what evidence triggered it, what safeguards followed, and what was explicitly left uncertain.
For one threshold you find, write down what an eval that tests it would actually have to measure — and why that is hard.
Skim the dangerous-capability evaluation paper (2403.13793) for what these evals look like as code rather than as policy prose.
Write half a page you could say out loud: what a safety case is, who it has to convince, and where evals sit inside it.

Sandbagging: when the eval is adversaria.desc: A model that underperforms on purpose breaks the core assumption of capability evaluation. Read the sandbagging paper for the threat model and the demonstrations, and understand why this makes elicitation — not measurement — the hard part of a dangerous-capability eval.
steps: Read arXiv 2406.07358 and separate the two threat models cleanly: the developer sandbagging the eval, and the model sandbagging on its own. They call for completely different countermeasures.
Note the uncomfortable demonstration: models can be made to hit a *target* score, not just a low one, which defeats naive 'suspiciously bad' detection.
Read the in-context scheming paper (2412.04984) for the behavioural evidence that strategic underperformance shows up without being trained in.

Design one detector and try it on a model you control: fine-tune or prompt a model to underperform on a subset, then see whether consistency checks, log-prob analysis, or password-unlocking recovers the true score.
Write down what your detector cannot catch. That list is the honest content of the section.
Read the anti-scheming stress-testing paper (2509.15541) for how far training-based mitigations currently get, and where they fail.

Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming (arXiv 2412.04984)
Stress Testing Deliberative Alignment for Anti-Scheming Training (arXiv 2509.15541)

Evaluation awareness.desc: Frontier models often detect that they are being evaluated, which means behaviour under test may not be behaviour in deployment. Read the evaluation-awareness paper, then look at your own agentic transcripts from Task 07 for the tells: unusually cautious refusals, meta-commentary about the task being a test, suspiciously tidy tool use.
steps: Read arXiv 2505.23836 and note the two distinct measurements: can the model tell it is being evaluated, and can it tell *what* is being tested.
Grep your Task 07 trajectories for explicit tells — 'this appears to be a test', 'as an evaluation scenario', hedged refusals on benign tasks — and count them as a rate, not an anecdote.

Run the paired experiment on your own harness: the same task with obvious eval scaffolding (synthetic names, tidy sandbox, canonical prompt) versus a deployment-shaped variant, and report the score difference with a CI.
Connect it to sandbagging: eval-awareness is the capability that makes strategic underperformance possible at all, so the two sections belong together in your writeup.
Note the design consequence for your own environment in Task 09: realistic file trees, plausible names, and no 'you are being evaluated' phrasing in the system prompt.
Write the paragraph on what this does to a capability number — it becomes a measurement of behaviour-under-observation, and you should say so in every report.

AI Sandbagging (arXiv 2406.07358)

Run one real safety eval and measure the.desc: Pick a task from inspect_evals, run it, then improve the scaffold — better prompting, more tools, more attempts — and measure how much the score moves. That delta is the elicitation gap, and it is why a single number from a weak scaffold is a lower bound on capability rather than a measurement of it.
steps: Install Inspect and inspect_evals and run one dangerous-capability or agentic eval unmodified, exactly as shipped. That is your baseline — record the exact command and version.
Read the task source. Inspect's API is async, so the solver, scorer and sandbox all compose as coroutines; understand the task/solver/scorer split before you change anything.
Improve elicitation in three separate arms so you can attribute the gain: (1) better system prompt and few-shot, (2) more/better tools, (3) best-of-k with more attempts.
Report each arm's score with a paired CI against the baseline. The largest arm is your headline elicitation gap.
Read METR's capability-elicitation guidelines and check your procedure against their list of failure checks — most first attempts under-elicit in an obvious documented way.
Write the conclusion in the framing the field uses: this number is a lower bound at this elicitation effort, and here is what more effort bought.

Ask what your environment would miss.desc: Work out what a model could get away with while scoring well on your tasks, and whether you would ever know.
steps: Describe a concrete way to score highly on your environment while doing something you would not endorse.
Check whether your verifier would catch it, and say so honestly if it would not.
Consider sandbagging: could a model deliberately underperform here, and would you detect it?
Check whether your task text signals that this is an evaluation — eval-aware behaviour is a measurement problem, not a curiosity.
Add the answers to the limitations section, including the ones you cannot currently answer.

Re-baseline it with real statistics.desc: Apply the week-27 statistics to the numbers you published in week 26. Expect several of them to move, and at least one to stop being significant.
steps: Compute the sample size needed for the effect size you actually care about, then run that many rather than the number that felt sufficient.
Use paired comparison where models see identical tasks — it removes most of the variance you were previously calling noise.
Put bootstrap confidence intervals on every headline number in the README.
Apply a multiple-comparison correction if you are reporting many model-versus-model claims at once.
Diff the new table against your v0 table and write a sentence on every number that moved.

papers.name: arXiv 2411.00640 — Adding Error Bars to Evals (Miller, Anthropic)

Add a validated judge, or justify not ha.desc: Subjective grading needs a judge you have measured. Fully programmatic grading needs an explicit statement that you chose it, not that you avoided the harder thing.
steps: If anything in your task is subjective, write the rubric and grade 50-100 samples by hand to create ground truth.
Report judge-human agreement, and measure position bias and length bias explicitly.
Re-check calibration against a held-out slice — judges drift as prompts and models change.
If your tasks are fully programmatic, state that in the README and say why that is right for this domain.
Record the judge model and version alongside the results; a judge upgrade silently changes every historical number.

papers.name: arXiv 2306.05685 — Judging LLM-as-a-Judge (MT-Bench, position and verbosity bias)
arXiv 2507.17746 — Rubrics as Rewards

Report reliability, not just accuracy.desc: The environment's own failure rate bounds every result anyone will ever get from it. Publish it as a first-class number.
steps: Run the same model on the same tasks at three to five seeds and publish per-task variance, not just the mean.
Separately count environment-side failures: setup flakes, timeouts, and verifier false negatives.
State the step budget and harness version with every number, since those are the parameters other people vary silently.
Add a reliability section to the README that a stranger can read before trusting anything else in it.
Re-run the whole thing on a clean machine to catch the state you did not know you depended on.

papers.name: arXiv 2604.17849 — On the Reliability of Computer Use Agents

Make it consumable by a training loop.desc: An eval scores a model; an environment can be trained against. The interface difference is what the job postings are asking for.
steps: Expose a clean reset with no hidden global state between episodes.
Make the reward dense enough to be learnable, and document what it does and does not credit.
Document the step budget and enforce it in code rather than by convention.
Run a short GRPO job against it using what you built in weeks 35-36, even if the result is bad — the point is that the interface holds.
Align the structure with the verifiers taskset/harness/runtime split so someone else's trainer can pick it up.

Publish v1 with a changelog against v0.desc: The visible delta between the week-26 version and this one is stronger evidence than either version alone.
steps: Tag v1 and write a changelog that names what v0 got wrong, not just what v1 adds.
Keep the v0 tag and its original README reachable — the naive version is part of the evidence.
Publish to the Environments Hub and check whether it qualifies for a bounty.
Write one short post walking through a number that changed and why, aimed at someone who does evals for a living.
Ask one person from your community to install it cold and tell you where they got stuck.

Pick a task you can verify without an LL.desc: Task selection is the hardest judgement call in evaluation and it happens before any code. Programmatic verifiability keeps version zero honest — you are testing your harness, not your grading.
steps: Choose a task family with objectively checkable answers: arithmetic with hidden state, structured extraction against ground truth, or code checked by execution.
Confirm it has real variance across models — trivially solved or universally failed tells you nothing.
Keep it narrow enough that a failure points at a specific cause you can name.
Write the verifier before the tasks; if you cannot state the check as code, pick a different task family.
Write down what this environment does NOT measure. That sentence goes in the README.

docs.name: Inspect — scorers, and when a programmatic check is enough

Write the four interfaces and nothing el.desc: Task, verifier, reset, reward. Resisting abstraction now is what lets version one exist at all.
steps: Implement the four interfaces against roughly twenty tasks. Twenty is plenty.
Point it at the served endpoint you stood up in week 21 so the loop is real rather than mocked.
Make it runnable in one command from a clean clone — if a stranger cannot run it, it is not published.
Write no config system, no plugin layer, and no abstraction for the second environment you have not built.
Read the verifiers library's taskset/harness/runtime split for the shape this converges on, but do not adopt the framework yet.

Run two models and write down the number.desc: Baselines exist first to prove the harness works end to end, and only second to be interesting.
steps: Run one small open model and one frontier API model across every task.
Record success rate, per-sample cost, tokens, and wall-clock — cost belongs beside accuracy from the very first run.
Do not tune prompts or scaffolding yet; you are measuring the harness, not competing.
Save the raw outputs, not just the aggregates. You will want them in week 32 when you learn to audit.
Note anything that made you uneasy about the numbers; that list becomes your Phase 2 backlog.

Publish it and say it is version zero.desc: Publishing something you know is flawed, with the flaws named, reads as competence. Publishing nothing until it is perfect reads as nothing at all.
steps: Push the repo public with a one-command quickstart and your baseline table in the README.
Write a Known limitations section that is specific: no variance estimates yet, no judge validation, small n, single seed.
Post it in the community you joined in week 1 and ask one concrete question about it.
Tag the commit v0 so the diff against your week-38 version is legible to a reviewer.
Put the repo link in your application materials now, not when it is finished.
